Finally, differences in volumetric energy density are important to note because fuels with lower volumetric energy density, such as LH , require more shipments (via truck or ship) to 2 deliver the same amount of energy, impacting supply chain logistics and airport operations. Similarly to cryogenic storage tanks on board tanker truckers or ocean carriers, stationary storage tanks for LH , LNG, and LE also use different tank materials, safety designs, and insulation 2 approaches based on fuel properties. Additionally, for the same cryogenic fuel, not all fixed and mobile storage tanks will use the exact same materials and design, as factors such as tank size, boil-off tolerance, and weight constraints also play a role. One thing that stays the same with 63 This report is available at no cost from the National Laboratory of the Rockies at www.nlr.gov/publications. stationary storage tank designs across each cryogenic fuel type is the desire to minimize the surface-area-to-volume ratio. The reason to choose a lower ratio is because it reduces heat leak into the tanks and thus lowers the rate of boil-off. This is why most cryogenic storage tanks, no matter what fuel, are usually found in cylindrical or spherical shapes. Surface-to-volume ratio can also be reduced by making tanks larger, but tanks can only be built so large before they become cost prohibitive or otherwise impractical. Unlike mobile cryogenic storage tanks, stationary cryogenic tanks require offset distances from surrounding permanent infrastructure for safety purposes. For LH and LNG, these offset 2 distances are defined in National Fire Protection Association (NFPA) NFPA 2 (NFPA 2026a) and NFPA 59A (NFPA 2026b) codes, respectively. There is not a code that is specific to LE, but offset distances in NFPA 58 (liquefied petroleum gases) may apply (NFPA 2024a). These codes require larger offset distances as storage tank volume increases, where exact distances are determined using careful experimentation and simulation that consider fuel properties such as flammability and explosivity to minimize safety risks.
